newsitem.title: USA: Clinton condemns shooting of seven Israeli girls.
newsitem.headline: Clinton condemns shooting of seven Israeli girls.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Thursday condemned the shooting of seven Israeli schoolgirls by a Jordanian soldier as "inexcusable and tragic" but said there was no evidence the killings were politically motivated and appealed for calm in the region.

"Today along the normally peaceful border between Israel and Jordan we have seen an inexcusable and tragic act of violence against schoolchildren. I condemn this act in the strongest possible terms," Clinton said.

Speaking as he left the White House for a visit to North Carolina, Clinton added: "There is no evidence at this moment that this terrible incident is related to the tensions in the area over the issues.
"For all we know this may have been just a deranged person," he said. "We have no reason to believe that this was politically motivated."
A Jordanian soldier on Thursday shot dead seven Israeli schoolgirls who were on a field trip to an Israeli-Jordanian border site called "The Island of Peace."

The soldier trained his automatic rifle on the girls, aged about 13, as they looked across the River Jordan to Syria and the Golan Heights. Israeli officials said the man, who was overpowered by other soldiers, appeared to be acting alone.

A White House spokeswoman said Clinton spoke to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu from Air Force One for 10 minutes to convey his condolences over the killings, which occurred amid growing tensions in the region.

A series of events, including Israel's decision to build new housing for Jews in Arab East Jerusalem and to hand over less West Bank territory than the Palestinians had expected, have badly strained relations in the region.

Earlier this week the king sent Netanyahu an anguished letter about the peace process, suggesting he had lost trust in his Israeli counterpart and warning him of the potential for violence in the region.

"I could remain aloof if the very lives of all Arabs and Israelis and their future were not fast sliding towards an abyss of bloodshed, brought about by fear and despair," the king said in the letter.

Hussein had been scheduled to meet Clinton in Washington on Tuesday, the fourth in a series of visits here by Middle East leaders to revive the peace process, but a Jordanian official told Israel radio the king would delay the visit.
White House officials said they had not been officially informed of whether Hussein still planned to make the visit, but said they would understand if he chose not to.
Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak met Clinton on Monday and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat the week before. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu met Clinton on Feb. 13.
Clinton said that no one should jump to any conclusions about the shooting, "given King Hussein and Jordan's long record of reaching for peace and reconciliation."

"We don't have the facts. None of us have any facts other than that we know this incident has occurred," he said. "We have no reason to believe this was politically motivated by any larger group or anything. We just don't know that."
And he urged leaders in the region to redouble their efforts for peace.

"Now the leaders in the region must work hard to calm the situation, to do everything in their power to create an atmosphere in which violence is rejected rather than embraced. We call on the leaders of the people of the region to reject violence, to redouble their efforts toward peace and reconciliation," he said.
